title: Cryptographic return value is unchecked
summary: The caller ignores a failure or partial-success result from key generation, encryption, decryption, signing, verification, or randomness.
applicable_when: A cryptographic API can fail or return a status.
check: Trace every return, exception, output length, and finalization result into caller control flow.
evidence: A call result is discarded or execution continues with uninitialized/stale output.
impact: Security checks can fail open or weak/default material can be used.
remediation: Require explicit success before consuming output and erase/abort on every failure.

title: Algorithm or mode defaults are security-sensitive
summary: A convenience API silently selects ECB, legacy padding, weak digest, provider-dependent behavior, or insecure parameters.
applicable_when: A cryptographic operation omits explicit algorithm parameters.
check: Resolve defaults for the exact library/version/provider and inspect runtime configuration.
evidence: A security property depends on an implicit or environment-dependent default.
impact: Updates or provider changes can weaken behavior or make protection differ across nodes.
remediation: Select an approved complete construction and all security-relevant parameters explicitly.

title: Key, nonce, and tag lengths are not validated
summary: Untrusted or derived lengths are truncated, padded, or accepted outside the construction profile.
applicable_when: Callers supply variable-length cryptographic inputs.
check: Test zero, short, long, and boundary lengths at every API boundary.
evidence: Implicit truncation/padding or successful operation with disallowed lengths.
impact: Effective strength drops or components interpret the operation differently.
remediation: Validate exact profile lengths before calling the primitive and reject all others.

title: Provider or backend selection can downgrade cryptography
summary: Configuration, environment, plugin order, or attacker-controlled identifiers select an unintended crypto provider.
applicable_when: The runtime supports multiple providers/backends.
check: Trace provider loading, priority, fallback, and algorithm name resolution.
evidence: An unapproved backend or implementation handles a security-critical operation.
impact: Security and validation assumptions may not hold for the selected implementation.
remediation: Pin approved providers, authenticate configuration, and fail closed when unavailable.

references.title: FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules

title: Cryptographic operation aliases input and output unsafely
summary: In-place buffers overlap in a way the API does not guarantee, corrupting nonces, tags, or plaintext.
applicable_when: Low-level APIs accept caller-managed buffers.
check: Inspect aliasing contracts and exercise exact/partial overlaps.
evidence: Overlapping buffers outside documented guarantees or corrupted authentication inputs.
impact: Corruption can disable verification, leak data, or create nondeterministic failures.
remediation: Use disjoint buffers unless the API explicitly guarantees the exact in-place operation.

title: Partial cryptographic output survives failure
summary: Buffers retain plaintext, keystream, candidate secrets, or unauthenticated output after an operation fails.
applicable_when: An API writes output before returning an error.
check: Force tag, padding, key, and RNG failures and inspect all output buffers/callbacks.
evidence: Security-sensitive partial output remains readable or is later reused.
impact: Attackers or later code can consume unauthenticated plaintext or secret remnants.
remediation: Treat outputs as invalid until success and clear them on every failure.

title: Secret comparison exits early
summary: A byte/string comparison stops at the first mismatch for MACs, tags, tokens, or secret-derived values.
applicable_when: An attacker can obtain repeated timings or co-locate with the process.
check: Inspect generated code or measure mismatch-position timing after controlling noise.
evidence: Runtime varies with the matching secret prefix.
impact: Attackers may recover authenticators or secret values incrementally.
remediation: Use a vetted constant-time comparison after fixed public length checks.

title: Control flow depends on secret data
summary: Branches, loop counts, exceptions, or early exits vary with key bits, nonces, plaintext secrets, or intermediate values.
applicable_when: Attackers can observe timing, branch predictors, power, or shared execution resources.
check: Trace tainted secret data through branches and benchmark controlled inputs.
evidence: A secret-dependent path produces a stable observable difference.
impact: Repeated observations can reveal secret material.
remediation: Use constant-time algorithms and verify compiled code on supported targets.

title: Memory access pattern depends on secret data
summary: Lookup-table indices, cache lines, page accesses, or gather/scatter addresses are secret-dependent.
applicable_when: Attackers can observe cache/page behavior or share hardware.
check: Inspect table lookups and memory traces for secret-indexed addresses.
evidence: Secret-controlled address selection in a cryptographic operation.
impact: Cache or microarchitectural observations can reveal keys.
remediation: Use constant-time table-free implementations or platform instructions with reviewed leakage properties.

title: Variable-time big-integer path handles secrets
summary: Private scalars or exponents use algorithms whose reductions, multiplication, or inversion timing depends on value.
applicable_when: General-purpose big integers implement private-key operations.
check: Identify secret operands and the exact multiplication/reduction/inversion routines.
evidence: A variable-time routine receives private exponent/scalar material.
impact: Timing or microarchitectural traces may recover private keys.
remediation: Use hardened constant-time private-key routines with appropriate blinding.

title: Compiler optimization breaks constant-time intent
summary: Source-level masking or comparisons compile into branches, optimized-away wipes, or target-specific variable-time instructions.
applicable_when: Custom constant-time or zeroization code is compiled across targets/optimizations.
check: Inspect disassembly and measure each supported compiler/architecture build.
evidence: Generated code violates the intended constant-time or wipe behavior.
impact: The implementation leaks despite apparently safe source.
remediation: Use vetted primitives and regression-check generated code and timing per supported toolchain.

title: Length or format discrepancies reveal secret state
summary: Response size, error text, retry count, connection closure, or resource use differs by secret-dependent validation outcome.
applicable_when: Attackers can submit chosen inputs and observe more than elapsed time.
check: Cluster all externally visible outcomes for valid and invalid classes.
evidence: A stable discrepancy maps to an internal padding, tag, key, or identity result.
impact: The discrepancy can become a decryption, membership, or credential oracle.
remediation: Unify externally observable failure behavior and perform sensitive validation in hardened code.

title: Custom cryptographic primitive replaces a reviewed construction
summary: Security relies on proprietary mixing, XOR, encoding, permutation, or novel algorithm without public analysis.
applicable_when: A nonstandard algorithm provides confidentiality, integrity, derivation, or signatures.
check: Recover the full construction and look for a standard primitive/profile it replaces.
evidence: Security-critical bespoke transformation with no recognized proof or review.
impact: Unknown structural weaknesses can permit trivial or unexpected attacks.
remediation: Replace it with a standardized, maintained construction matched to the threat model.

title: Standard primitives are composed without a defined protocol
summary: Individually sound hashes, ciphers, MACs, and signatures are combined ad hoc without domain separation or a security model.
applicable_when: The target defines its own protected message or handshake format.
check: Document exact ordering, keys, encodings, errors, and adversary capabilities.
evidence: No standard profile or analysis covers the complete composition.
impact: Cross-protocol, replay, oracle, and binding failures can defeat all component primitives.
remediation: Adopt a reviewed protocol or obtain specialist review of a precise specification and test vectors.

title: Cryptographic test vectors cover only happy paths
summary: Tests prove interoperability but omit malformed, boundary, state-reuse, concurrency, and negative verification cases.
applicable_when: The implementation has security-critical custom glue or parsers.
check: Review tests for negative inputs, state transitions, cross-implementation vectors, and failure invariants.
evidence: Only successful known-answer cases are tested.
impact: Regressions in rejection and state handling can silently introduce vulnerabilities.
remediation: Add adversarial, boundary, differential, and stateful tests alongside known-answer vectors.

references.title: FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules

title: RSA CRT result is released without recombination verification
summary: A transient fault in one CRT branch can produce a faulty signature or decryption result.
applicable_when: Attackers can induce faults or collect naturally faulty private operations.
check: Inspect CRT implementation and test injected branch faults.
evidence: CRT output returned without verifying it against the public operation.
impact: One faulty signature can permit RSA private-key factor recovery.
remediation: Verify the CRT result before release and use hardened fault countermeasures.

title: Signature generation lacks fault resistance
summary: Faults in nonce generation, hashing, scalar multiplication, or encoding can leak a signing key or create attacker-useful signatures.
applicable_when: Physical, voltage, clock, rowhammer, or fault-prone environments are relevant.
check: Model faults at each signing stage and compare released outputs.
evidence: Faulty signatures are returned without redundancy or verification.
impact: Differential or algebraic analysis may recover the private key.
remediation: Use hardened implementations, redundancy, and verify generated signatures before release.

references.title: FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules

title: KEM decapsulation fault changes externally visible behavior
summary: Faulted decapsulation bypasses ciphertext checks or exposes whether internal re-encryption matched.
applicable_when: Attackers can induce faults during KEM decapsulation or compare many outcomes.
check: Inject faults around validation, implicit rejection, and secret selection.
evidence: Fault-dependent errors, secrets, or protocol behavior escape the boundary.
impact: Fault queries can undermine chosen-ciphertext security or reveal private information.
remediation: Use hardened decapsulation with redundant checks and indistinguishable failure handling.

references.title: FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules

title: Boot or self-test failure leaves cryptography operational
summary: Known-answer, integrity, entropy, or conditional self-test failure is logged but operations continue.
applicable_when: The module performs startup or conditional cryptographic self-tests.
check: Force each failure and trace all exposed operations afterward.
evidence: Keys or cryptographic services remain available after a critical self-test failure.
impact: A corrupted or defective primitive may protect data without its claimed properties.
remediation: Enter a persistent error state and block cryptographic operations until securely recovered.

references.title: FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules

title: Secrets are written to logs or telemetry
summary: Keys, nonces with key context, passwords, plaintext, seeds, or decrypted tokens enter logs, traces, metrics, or crash reports.
applicable_when: Diagnostics can observe cryptographic inputs, outputs, or context.
check: Search logging call arguments and inspect real support bundles/crash reports.
evidence: Recoverable secret material in diagnostic sinks.
impact: Log readers or third parties can decrypt, forge, or impersonate.
remediation: Redact by construction, prohibit secret-bearing types from logging, and purge exposed records.

references.title: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

title: Secrets remain in pageable memory or crash dumps without need
summary: Long-lived private material is broadly present in process dumps, swap, hibernation, or debugger-accessible memory.
applicable_when: The threat model includes local capture, crash collection, or shared hosts.
check: Inspect allocation duration, locking, dump policy, child inheritance, and copies.
evidence: Secret buffers in dumps/swap or inherited into unrelated processes.
impact: Operational artifacts or local access reveal long-term credentials.
remediation: Minimize residency/copies and apply platform-appropriate protected memory and dump controls.

references.title: CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information

title: Secret zeroization is incomplete or optimized away
summary: Cleanup misses copies, runs only on success, or is removed by the compiler.
applicable_when: Temporary secret buffers outlive their use.
check: Inspect all exits and generated code; scan memory after operation and failure.
evidence: Recoverable secret bytes after the documented lifetime.
impact: Later disclosure recovers secrets assumed erased.
remediation: Use supported explicit-zero APIs and cleanup on every path while minimizing copies.

references.title: CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information

title: Secret-dependent allocation or paging leaks information
summary: Allocation size, object lifetime, page faults, GC behavior, or swapping correlates with secret values.
applicable_when: Managed runtimes, enclaves, or observable memory pressure process secrets.
check: Profile allocation/page traces across controlled secret inputs.
evidence: Stable memory-behavior differences tied to secret data.
impact: Observers can infer secret length, structure, or values.
remediation: Use fixed-shape processing and isolate secret handling in reviewed primitives.

title: Padding validity is externally distinguishable
summary: CBC or padded asymmetric decryption exposes whether padding was structurally correct.
applicable_when: Attackers can submit modified ciphertext repeatedly.
check: Mutate blocks and compare timing, errors, retries, and side effects.
evidence: A reliable signal separates valid from invalid padding.
impact: Adaptive queries may decrypt ciphertext or forge protected messages.
remediation: Use AEAD or a secure KEM; otherwise apply protocol-specific constant-time implicit rejection.

references.title: Security Flaws Induced by CBC Padding — Applications to SSL, IPSEC, WTLS

title: Authentication validity is distinguishable before authorization
summary: Tag/MAC/signature failures differ from later parsing, account, or policy failures in a queryable way.
applicable_when: Attackers can test candidate protected objects.
check: Compare all observable outcomes across failure stages.
evidence: A reliable distinction reveals whether a cryptographic check passed.
impact: Attackers may validate guesses, enumerate protected state, or amplify another attack.
remediation: Minimize pre-authentication behavior and coalesce externally visible failures where the protocol permits.

title: Decrypted plaintext is parsed before authentication
summary: Length, allocation, decompression, decoding, or business logic runs on attacker-modified unauthenticated plaintext.
applicable_when: The construction authenticates ciphertext but the implementation streams plaintext early.
check: Trace dataflow and side effects before final authentication success.
evidence: Parser calls, allocations, logs, or errors based on unauthenticated plaintext.
impact: Attackers can extract information, trigger vulnerabilities, or alter state despite failed authentication.
remediation: Buffer and authenticate completely before parsing or exposing plaintext.

title: Key-existence or recipient oracle is exposed
summary: Behavior reveals whether a key ID, private key, user key, or recipient successfully processed an encrypted object.
applicable_when: Attackers can submit objects for selected recipients/key identifiers.
check: Compare responses for absent, disabled, wrong, and valid keys while equalizing input.
evidence: Observable differences identify valid keys, users, or recipients.
impact: Attackers can enumerate security principals or focus cryptanalytic queries.
remediation: Authenticate requests earlier where possible and normalize lookup/decryption failure behavior.

title: Nonce or counter update is not atomic
summary: Concurrent encryptions can reserve the same nonce/counter before either persists the increment.
applicable_when: Multiple threads/processes share a key and nonce state.
check: Stress concurrent encryption and inspect reservation/commit ordering.
evidence: Duplicate key/nonce pairs or a non-atomic read-increment-write path.
impact: Stream/AEAD security can fail catastrophically.
remediation: Allocate nonce ranges atomically or use a concurrency-safe per-key state service.

references.title: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization

title: Rollback restores nonce, counter, or key state
summary: VM snapshot, backup restore, firmware rollback, transaction abort, or clock rollback repeats cryptographic state.
applicable_when: Persistent cryptographic state can be restored to an earlier version.
check: Restore snapshots/backups and compare generated nonces, epochs, and active keys.
evidence: A post-restore key/nonce or sequence value duplicates prior use.
impact: Nonce reuse, replay acceptance, or retired-key resurrection can break security.
remediation: Bind state to monotonic epochs, rekey after restore, and design rollback-resistant persistence.

references.title: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization

title: Partial persistence creates key/state mismatch
summary: Crash ordering persists a key without its nonce counter, or vice versa, producing reuse or undecryptable records.
applicable_when: Key and associated counters/epochs persist separately.
check: Inject crashes at each update boundary and recover.
evidence: Recovered state combines an old counter with an active key or inconsistent epochs.
impact: Security may fail through nonce reuse or availability loss.
remediation: Persist related cryptographic state atomically or use derivation/epochs that make partial commits safe.

references.title: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization

title: Rate limits are not scoped to the cryptographic key
summary: Forgery, password, decryption-oracle, or signature attempts can be distributed across nodes or reset by reconnecting.
applicable_when: Security bounds assume a maximum number of adversarial attempts per key.
check: Trace counters across sessions, nodes, tenants, and key rotation.
evidence: Attempts exceed the design bound through sharding or reset.
impact: Online guessing or forgery probability exceeds the construction's assumptions.
remediation: Enforce limits across the whole key/security domain and rotate or lock safely when reached.
